stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 34 plus 3 weeks gestation is admitted from clinic with a headache and epigastric pain. Her blood pressure recorded three times over 30 minutes is 168/112, 172/108 and 170/110. She has 3+ proteinuria on dipstick and a spot protein to creatinine ratio of 65 mg/mmol (less than 30). She has brisk lower limb reflexes with 4 beats of clonus on the right.

On examination she is uncomfortable but alert. Uterine tone is soft, cardiotocography is normal with a reactive trace, and there are no vaginal loss or contractions. Full blood count shows a platelet count of 135 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 90 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90) and lactate dehydrogenase 340 U/L (less than 250). Antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturation were given three days ago in another episode of admission.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure 170/110, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, fetal heart rate 145
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), platelets 135 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), ALT 90 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90), LDH 340 U/L (less than 250), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.36)

lead_in: In addition to intravenous antihypertensive therapy, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose as an alternative to magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis
Administer intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg as a repeat antenatal corticosteroid dose for lung maturation
Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg as diuretic therapy for suspected preeclampsia-related pulmonary oedema
Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour maintenance infusion
Administer intravenous diazepam 10 mg as a prophylactic anticonvulsant while transfer to a tertiary unit is arranged

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin timing after sensitising event
stem:
A 24-year-old primigravida at 22 weeks gestation presents 6 hours after a minor motor vehicle crash. She was a restrained front seat passenger in a low-speed rear-ending collision, has no abdominal pain, no per vaginal bleeding, no uterine tenderness on palpation and a reassuring cardiotocography trace. Fetal biometry is appropriate for gestation on point-of-care ultrasound with an anterior placenta well clear of the internal os.

Her booking blood group is O rhesus negative with no red cell antibodies detected at 28 week screen (which has not yet been performed at her current gestation). She has previously declined the 28-week prophylactic anti-D dose plan but consents today to being managed as clinically indicated. She is otherwise well and has no other injuries.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 122 g/L (115-165), blood group O rhesus negative, indirect antiglobulin test negative, Kleihauer-Betke test pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding anti-D immunoglobulin?

options.text: Await the Kleihauer-Betke test result before deciding whether to administer any anti-D immunoglobulin at all
Administer intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU now given the minor severity of the mechanism of injury
Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin because the placenta is anterior and the motor vehicle mechanism is very low grade
Administer intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin 1500 IU now as a routine 28 week prophylactic dose in advance
Administer intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU now and await Kleihauer-Betke to guide any additional dose

stem:
A 32-year-old woman with a body mass index of 26 attends a diabetes in pregnancy clinic at 27 weeks gestation after a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed at 26 weeks in her local pathology lab. Her fasting glucose was 5.1 mmol/L, 1-hour glucose 9.8 mmol/L, and 2-hour glucose 8.3 mmol/L (fasting less than 5.1, 1-hour less than 10.0, 2-hour less than 8.5). She has no personal history of type 2 diabetes, no polycystic ovary syndrome, and her first pregnancy 3 years ago was uncomplicated with a birth weight of 3300 g.

Her first-trimester screening glucose was normal. Booking bloods showed normal HbA1c at 5.3 percent (under 5.7). She is asymptomatic with no polyuria or polydipsia. Fetal biometry at 27 weeks shows appropriate growth with abdominal circumference on the 60th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 5.1 mmol/L (less than 5.1), 1-hour 9.8 mmol/L (less than 10.0), 2-hour 8.3 mmol/L (less than 8.5), HbA1c 5.3 percent (less than 5.7)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic interpretation and next step?

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes based on the fasting value meeting the threshold and commence structured dietary advice and self blood glucose monitoring
Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in 4 weeks because none of the individual values definitively exceeded the diagnostic thresholds today
Reassure that gestational diabetes is excluded because at least two values are required to meet the diagnostic thresholds under the ADIPS pathway
Diagnose overt diabetes in pregnancy based on the OGTT results and commence subcutaneous insulin as first-line pharmacotherapy today
Repeat the HbA1c and treat as gestational diabetes only if the result rises to at least 6.5 percent on the follow-up sample

subtopic_detail: Postpartum haemorrhage escalation beyond first-line uterotonics
stem:
A 33-year-old multiparous woman has just delivered a live infant weighing 4200 g vaginally after a 60 minute second stage and active management of the third stage with intramuscular oxytocin 10 units. Estimated blood loss at 10 minutes postpartum is 1200 mL from ongoing dark red bleeding per vagina with a boggy fundus at the level of the umbilicus.

Examination under good lighting demonstrates an intact perineum and second-degree perineal tear that has been repaired without ongoing bleeding from the wound. The lower uterine segment is empty on bimanual examination and the placenta was inspected and reported as complete. Bimanual uterine compression and a further intravenous oxytocin 10 unit slow bolus with intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram have been given but the fundus remains soft and bleeding continues at 200 mL per 5 minutes. Blood pressure is 92/58 with pulse rate 122. There is no history of hypertension, coronary disease, or asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 122, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165) on point-of-care testing, thromboelastography pending, blood group known O rhesus positive with active group and hold

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic step?

options.text: Administer repeat intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram as the second dose within 5 minutes of the first dose given
Administer intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram (repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses) with continuing bimanual compression
Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading bolus over 20 minutes for suspected retained postpartum uterine relaxation
Administer intramuscular oxytocin 10 units as a third dose to overcome the persistent atony via peripheral receptor upregulation
Administer intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g slow bolus alone and continue observation of uterine tone without further uterotonics

subtopic_detail: Recurrent APH from placenta praevia at 32 weeks
stem:
A 34-year-old woman gravida 3 para 2 with two prior lower segment caesarean sections presents at 32 weeks gestation with her second episode of painless vaginal bleeding this admission. The previous episode was 5 days ago and settled after 200 mL of loss with a course of intramuscular betamethasone commenced at that time (second dose given 24 hours ago). She has been inpatient since.

Today she has passed approximately 400 mL of fresh red blood over 30 minutes with a soft, non-tender uterus. Fetal biometry a week ago showed appropriate growth. A repeat cardiotocograph is reactive with baseline 145 with normal variability and no decelerations. Her booking transvaginal ultrasound confirmed a complete placenta praevia with a posterior placenta covering the internal os; there was no ultrasound evidence of a morbidly adherent placenta but this was not formally excluded on MRI.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 104, blood pressure 108/68, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, fetal heart rate 145
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 96 g/L (115-165) (was 110 g/L one week ago), platelets 220 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), coagulation studies within normal limits, blood group A rhesus positive with two units crossmatched and available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Attempt vaginal delivery after amniotomy and syntocinon augmentation once corticosteroids are complete and bleeding settles again
Insert an intrauterine balloon tamponade device to control bleeding and continue expectant management to at least 37 weeks
Arrange delivery by elective caesarean section under general anaesthesia within the next 24 hours after multidisciplinary team review
Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate as neuroprotection and continue expectant management targeting delivery at 34 weeks gestation
Administer intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g and repeat the transvaginal ultrasound to reconfirm the placental location today

subtopic_detail: Historical bilaterality flip in ectopic surgical choice
stem:
A 34-year-old woman gravida 3 para 1 presents to a regional emergency department with 4 hours of severe right iliac fossa pain, dizziness and one episode of syncope. On arrival she is pale, cool peripherally with a heart rate of 128 and blood pressure of 88/50. She has abdominal guarding maximal in the right iliac fossa, and cervical excitation on gentle speculum examination. Point-of-care ultrasound in ED shows a moderate volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas and no intrauterine pregnancy.

Her past history includes a laparoscopic LEFT salpingectomy 3 years ago for a ruptured left tubal ectopic and a subsequent spontaneous term vaginal delivery 18 months ago. Her right fallopian tube was visualised as intact at the previous operation. She has had no fertility treatment. Serum beta hCG on arrival is 6800 IU/L. Two units of crossmatched blood are available and initial resuscitation has been commenced. She and her partner have consented in principle to whatever surgery is needed to save life.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 88/50, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: beta hCG 6800 IU/L, haemoglobin 88 g/L (115-165) (was 128 g/L one month ago), platelets 220 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), blood group A rhesus positive
data_table.Operative findings: at laparoscopy: 500 mL of intraperitoneal blood, ruptured right ampullary ectopic with active bleeding, left fallopian tube absent (prior salpingectomy), otherwise normal uterus and right ovary

lead_in: What is the most appropriate operative procedure?

options.text: Proceed with right salpingostomy to preserve the only remaining tube for the possibility of future natural conception attempts
Perform emergency laparotomy with total abdominal hysterectomy for definitive haemorrhage control in the shocked patient
Administer intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 and close the abdomen without proceeding to definitive resection today
Proceed with right salpingectomy to control haemorrhage and prevent same-tube recurrence in the only remaining tube
Perform right salpingotomy with placement of a subtubal ligation to prevent same tube recurrence in future cycles

stem:
A 32-year-old G2P1 has just delivered a 3900 g baby vaginally after a spontaneous labour and second stage of 40 minutes. Twenty minutes after birth she has ongoing bright red vaginal bleeding estimated at 1000 mL with clot expression. Her uterus feels soft and bulky above the umbilicus.

She has already received 10 units of intramuscular oxytocin as third-stage prophylaxis and the placenta was delivered complete. Her booking blood pressure was 118/72 mmHg. She had no antenatal hypertension and has taken no cardiovascular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus above umbilicus, actively bleeding; placenta delivered complete; no cervical or vaginal tears identified on inspection
data_table.Investigations: Group and hold sent, cross-match ordered; venous access with two 16G cannulae; oxytocin infusion prepared

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms with intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g
Intramuscular carboprost 250 micrograms into the deltoid with continued oxytocin
Intravenous ergometrine 500 micrograms slow push with continuous oxytocin infusion
Sublingual misoprostol 800 micrograms and observe for uterine tone response
Intramuscular oxytocin 10 units second dose with continuous oxytocin infusion 40 units

stem:
A 28-year-old G2P1 presents to the early pregnancy unit at 6 weeks by LMP with right iliac fossa discomfort and vaginal spotting. She is haemodynamically stable and pain is mild. Serum beta hCG is 4200 IU/L.

Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterine cavity and a 2.6 cm right adnexal mass separate from the ovary with a yolk sac visible but no fetal pole and no cardiac activity. She has stopped breastfeeding her first child three months ago and is keen to avoid surgery if possible.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, comfortable at rest; mild right iliac fossa tenderness on palpation without guarding or rebound; no cervical excitation
data_table.Investigations: Beta hCG 4200 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115 to 165), liver and renal function within normal limits, no free fluid on ultrasound

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Expectant management with serial beta hCG measurement every 48 to 72 hours
Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected tube under the acute gynaecology list
Laparoscopic salpingostomy with preservation of the affected tube and cornual repair
Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 single dose with day 4 and day 7 hCG follow-up
Mifepristone 200 mg orally followed by misoprostol 800 micrograms vaginally at 48 hours

stem:
A 33-year-old G3P2 attends her 28-week antenatal appointment after a routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. She has been well throughout pregnancy with a normal 20-week morphology scan and appropriate fundal height. Her BMI at booking was 27 kg/m2 and her father has type 2 diabetes.

Her results are fasting glucose 5.2 mmol/L, one-hour glucose 10.4 mmol/L and two-hour glucose 7.9 mmol/L. She reports no polyuria or polydipsia and her home glucose monitoring since triage has shown fasting values ranging from 4.6 to 4.9 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 28 cm at 28 weeks, longitudinal cephalic presentation, fetal movements normal
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 5.2 mmol/L, 1 hour 10.4 mmol/L, 2 hour 7.9 mmol/L; HbA1c 5.4 percent (below 5.7)

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic interpretation and next step?

options.text: GDM diagnosed on fasting glucose criterion, refer for immediate insulin commencement
GDM diagnosed on the 1 hour value; start lifestyle plus home glucose monitoring
Normal test; reassure and no further monitoring or intervention required in this pregnancy
Overt diabetes in pregnancy; refer for endocrinology-led insulin initiation this week
Impaired glucose tolerance; repeat 75 g OGTT in four weeks with same thresholds applied

stem:
A 26-year-old G1P0 attends her 28-week antenatal appointment. Her blood group at booking was O rhesus D negative and her antibody screen was negative. Her partner is known to be rhesus D positive. She has had no vaginal bleeding, no antenatal invasive procedures, and no abdominal trauma this pregnancy.

She is asymptomatic today with a normal midwifery review. Fundal height and fetal heart tones are unremarkable. She asks about routine anti-D administration.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 110/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 28 cm at 28 weeks; longitudinal lie, cephalic presentation; fetal movements reported normal
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O rhesus D negative; antibody screen negative at 28 weeks; midstream urine and full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anti-D dosing schedule?

options.text: Anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU intramuscular now, one further dose at delivery
Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscular at 34 weeks only, plus post-delivery dose
Anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU intramuscular now and again at 34 weeks
Anti-D immunoglobulin 1500 IU intramuscular now as a single-dose regimen
No anti-D required unless a sensitising event occurs before delivery

stem:
A 34-year-old G3P2 at 33 weeks gestation presents with sudden onset of moderate painless bright red vaginal bleeding while at rest. Her previous births were two lower segment caesarean sections. Her 20-week morphology scan reported an anterior placenta reaching to the internal os.

She has soaked one large pad. Fetal movements have been active throughout. She has had no abdominal trauma, no contractions and no ruptured membranes. She last ate two hours ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min baseline with normal variability
data_table.Examination: Soft, non-tender abdomen; uterus relaxed between reassuring fetal movements; speculum deferred pending imaging
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and group and hold sent; CTG reactive with reassuring baseline; large-bore IV access secured

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next single step?

options.text: Digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilation and any presenting cord
Speculum examination in lithotomy after gentle betadine cleaning of the vulva
Immediate emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia in theatre
Kleihauer test only and outpatient follow-up given painless nature of bleed
Bedside transabdominal then transvaginal ultrasound to confirm placental position

stem:
A 30-year-old G2P1 attends the first-trimester ultrasound at 12 weeks after a spontaneous conception. Imaging shows twin fetuses with a single placental mass, a thin dividing membrane and no evidence of a lambda sign at the base. She has no personal or family history of twinning and did not use fertility treatment.

Both fetuses are appropriately grown for gestation with crown-rump lengths within 5 percent of each other. She is asymptomatic and reports normal fetal movements at this early stage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rates 168 and 172/min
data_table.Examination: Uterus corresponding with 12 to 14 weeks gestation; abdomen otherwise unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: monochorionic diamniotic twin pregnancy at 12 weeks; nuchal translucency 1.8 mm and 1.9 mm; combined first trimester screen result pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate additional antenatal surveillance schedule?

options.text: Fortnightly ultrasound from 16 weeks for growth and amniotic fluid discordance
Four-weekly ultrasound from 20 weeks matching dichorionic diamniotic surveillance
Monthly maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein screening from 18 weeks to term
Weekly fetal heart auscultation from 24 weeks with routine standard ultrasound only
Weekly cardiotocography from 26 weeks with three-monthly growth scans thereafter

stem:
A 32-year-old woman is reviewed at her six-week postnatal check after her first birth. She scores 16 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale with a positive response to item 10 (thoughts of self-harm reported as fleeting, no plan, no intent). She is exclusively breastfeeding a well-thriving infant.

She describes anhedonia, poor sleep beyond that expected with a newborn, and reduced appetite. She has no prior psychiatric history, is not on any medications, and has strong partner and family supports. She is willing to consider medication and continue breastfeeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert and cooperative; tearful when discussing infant care but engaged; no active psychosis; safety planning completed with partner
data_table.Investigations: EPDS 16; TSH 1.8 mIU/L (within normal limits); ferritin 42 mcg/L (within normal limits)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antidepressant?

options.text: Paroxetine 20 mg oral daily with weekly review during initial titration phase
Venlafaxine 75 mg oral daily with blood pressure monitoring in first month
Mirtazapine 30 mg oral nightly with weekly weight and sedation monitoring
Sertraline 50 mg oral daily with weekly review during initial titration phase
Fluoxetine 20 mg oral daily with monthly review for breastfeeding infant sedation

stem:
A 33-year-old G2P1 is at 41 weeks gestation, in active second stage. The head delivers but the anterior shoulder fails to deliver with the next contraction and turtle-neck sign is present. Additional help has already been called. The registrar has coached her out of the pushing position and drained the bladder. McRoberts position and suprapubic pressure have been applied for one contraction cycle without progress.

Her estimated fetal weight was 4.4 kg. This is her second delivery; her first infant was 3.8 kg vaginally without complication. She has an epidural in situ. Time from head delivery is now 90 seconds and the fetal heart rate is 100/min.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 108/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees C, fetal heart rate 100/min
data_table.Examination: Head fully delivered, turtle-neck sign persistent; McRoberts in position, suprapubic pressure applied; perineum intact so far
data_table.Investigations: None applicable; ongoing intrapartum team present including senior obstetrician on the way; paediatric team in room

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next manoeuvre?

options.text: Perform Zavanelli manoeuvre with cephalic replacement and immediate caesarean section
Enter the posterior vagina to deliver the posterior arm across the fetal chest
Apply strong axial traction to the fetal head with the mother in McRoberts
Perform symphysiotomy under local anaesthetic to widen the pelvic outlet
Turn the mother onto all fours (Gaskin manoeuvre) and re-attempt gentle traction only

subtopic_detail: Abdominal pain three days after methotrexate for a tubal ectopic
stem: A 27-year-old woman treated with methotrexate three days ago for a tubal ectopic pregnancy returns with lower abdominal pain that began this morning. She has not fainted and has no shoulder tip pain. Her abdomen is tender in the right iliac fossa without guarding.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 116/74, RR 16, T 36.8, SpO2 99 percent room air
data_table.Investigations: Hb 124 g/L, was 126 g/L; hCG 2,450 IU/L, day 0 was 2,200 IU/L
data_table.Ultrasound: Unchanged 20 mm right adnexal mass; small volume free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for observation with repeat haemoglobin and hCG
Transfer to theatre now for laparoscopic salpingectomy
Give a second dose of methotrexate and discharge her home
Discharge with oral analgesia and review in four days
Arrange computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis

stem:
A 32-year-old woman (G3P2) is 20 minutes postpartum after an unassisted vaginal delivery of a 4.1 kg baby at 40+3 weeks. Blood loss is measured at 1200 mL and continuing. Her placenta was delivered intact with controlled cord traction and Syntocinon 10 units IM was given at delivery of the anterior shoulder. Her third-stage bleeding continued and she has already had a Syntocinon 40 unit infusion started.

On bimanual examination the uterus is soft and above the umbilicus. There is no visible perineal, vaginal or cervical laceration on inspection. Her booking bloods showed haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160) with normal platelets and coagulation profile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and 2 cm above the umbilicus; no perineal, vaginal or cervical laceration on speculum inspection; bladder empty via indwelling catheter
data_table.Investigations: Two large-bore IV lines in situ; crossmatch sent; venous blood gas pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: IM ergometrine 250 micrograms and prepare for further uterotonic escalation
Repeat IM Syntocinon 10 units bolus with continued uterine massage
Intramyometrial carboprost 250 micrograms directly into the uterine fundus
Tranexamic acid 1 gram IV alone without any further uterotonic therapy
Insert a Bakri balloon and defer any additional uterotonic administration

subtopic_detail: Plateauing hCG after conservative tubal surgery
stem: A 32-year-old woman had a laparoscopic salpingostomy two weeks ago for a tubal ectopic pregnancy, chosen to preserve the tube. She is well, with no pain and normal observations, and attends for her weekly hCG result.

data_table.Serum hCG: Day 0: 1,900 IU/L; day 7: 420 IU/L; day 14: 380 IU/L
data_table.Investigations: Hb 122 g/L; creatinine 62 micromol/L; ALT 20 U/L
data_table.Ultrasound: No adnexal mass; empty uterus; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intramuscular methotrexate and continue weekly hCG
Repeat the hCG in four weeks with no other action
Proceed to laparoscopic salpingectomy of that tube
Arrange uterine curettage to exclude retained trophoblast
Start a course of oral misoprostol over the next three days

subtopic_detail: Severe pre-eclampsia magnesium and delivery timing
stem:
A 34-year-old primigravida is admitted at 34+2 weeks with a 24-hour history of frontal headache and epigastric discomfort. Her blood pressure at booking was 118/72. On arrival her blood pressure is 168/112 despite 20 mg oral nifedipine 30 minutes ago, then 154/98 after a second 20 mg dose. Urine dipstick shows 3+ protein and spot urine protein:creatinine is 82 mg/mmol.

She has +2 patellar hyperreflexia with no clonus. The fetus is active with a reactive CTG. She has no visual disturbance now and denies chest pain. She has had no antenatal steroids. Her husband is beside her and she has consented to admission and further investigations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 154/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15; +2 patellar reflexes bilaterally, no clonus; fundal height 34 cm; CTG reactive with baseline 145 and normal variability
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 108 x10^9/L (150-450); ALT 78 U/L (<40); creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90); LDH 340 U/L; spot urine protein:creatinine 82 mg/mmol (<30)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Betamethasone 11.4 mg IM as a single dose and immediate caesarean section
Commence intravenous labetalol 20 mg boluses and titrate to a systolic under 140
Administer IV magnesium sulfate 4 g bolus followed by a 1 g/hour infusion
Sodium nitroprusside infusion for tighter blood pressure control and re-review
Watchful monitoring on the antenatal ward with 4-hourly blood pressure charting

stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida was diagnosed with gestational diabetes at 26 weeks after a 75 gram OGTT showed a 1-hour value of 10.6 mmol/L. She has been on dietary and exercise therapy with a diabetes educator for 3 weeks and monitors capillary glucose fasting and 2 hours after each main meal.

She is now 29+3 weeks. Her recent 7-day glucose profile shows fasting values consistently 5.6-6.1 mmol/L and 2-hour postprandial values 7.4-8.1 mmol/L after breakfast, with acceptable readings after other meals. She is compliant with the diet plan and has gained 4 kg since booking. Fetal growth ultrasound at 28 weeks showed an estimated fetal weight on the 62nd centile with normal liquor and Dopplers.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft; fundal height 30 cm; fetal movements reported as normal
data_table.Investigations: Home glucose profile as above; HbA1c 5.6 percent (nondiabetic under 5.7); no ketonuria; renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her diabetes management?

options.text: Continue dietary and exercise therapy alone and repeat the profile after 2 weeks
Immediate induction of labour at 30 weeks to end pregnancy and eliminate the risk
Metformin 500 mg twice daily titrated to 1 gram twice daily over 2 weeks
Commence isophane insulin 0.1 units/kg at bedtime and titrate to fasting target
Rapid-acting insulin aspart at each meal only with no basal insulin cover

stem:
A 33-year-old woman (G2P1) is 34+0 weeks with placenta praevia identified on her routine morphology scan at 20 weeks. A follow-up transvaginal scan at 32 weeks confirmed the placental edge covers the internal cervical os. She has had two small self-limiting antepartum bleeds at 30 and 33 weeks, each settling within 12 hours without further intervention.

Her previous pregnancy was a term uncomplicated vaginal delivery of a 3.2 kg baby with no operative history. She is blood group O positive with negative antibody screen. She has no coagulopathy and no prior uterine surgery. She has completed her Anti-D course and had betamethasone at the time of the second bleed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 142/min
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, non-tender, fundal height 34 cm; no active vaginal bleeding on speculum; cervix closed and long
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-160); platelets 220 x10^9/L (150-450); blood group O positive antibody negative; group and hold current

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: External cephalic version at 37 weeks followed by trial of vaginal delivery at term
Await spontaneous labour and reassess placental position digitally at term
Immediate caesarean section today under regional anaesthesia in the operating theatre
Planned induction of labour at 39 weeks with epidural once cervix is favourable for use
Planned elective caesarean section at 36+0 to 37+0 weeks with group-specific blood available

stem:
A 34-year-old woman attends for routine cervical screening. She has been screened regularly since age 25, with the last screen 5 years ago negative for HPV. She has no abnormal vaginal bleeding, no postcoital bleeding and no intermenstrual bleeding. She is on a combined oral contraceptive and has never been pregnant. She is fully vaccinated with Gardasil 9.

Her cervical screening test today returns HPV positive for non-16/18 oncogenic HPV. Reflex liquid-based cytology on the same sample is reported as negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She is well and works as a schoolteacher. She has no immunosuppression.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft; speculum shows a healthy pink cervix with no lesion or contact bleeding; bimanual exam unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening test: HPV positive (non 16/18); reflex LBC: negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat cervical screening test in 12 months to reassess HPV status and cytology together
Immediate colposcopic referral for directed biopsy of any abnormal transformation zone
Return to routine 5-year screening as she has previously screened negative for HPV
Refer to gynaecology for large loop excision of the transformation zone as prophylaxis
Test of cure by cervical smear alone in 6 months regardless of the HPV subtype result

stem:
A 58-year-old woman presents to your general practice with 3 weeks of intermittent light vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 6 years ago. She has never used menopausal hormone therapy and takes no other regular medications. She is otherwise well, BMI 27 kg/m2, has never been pregnant, and has no family history of endometrial or ovarian cancer.

You perform a transvaginal ultrasound in the same visit which shows an endometrial thickness of 6 mm with a heterogeneous appearance. Both ovaries are quiescent and there is no free fluid. She has no personal history of breast cancer and has never used tamoxifen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 122/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable mass; speculum shows a small amount of old blood in the posterior fornix and a smooth pink cervix; bimanual exam unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound: endometrial thickness 6 mm, heterogeneous; ovaries normal; no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat transvaginal ultrasound in 3 months to observe any endometrial change over time
Pipelle endometrial biopsy in the outpatient clinic for histological assessment now
Colposcopy with directed cervical biopsy of any acetowhite areas visualised
Serum CA125 measurement and CT abdomen/pelvis before any tissue diagnosis is sought
Empirical continuous progestogen without any histological sampling of the endometrium

stem:
A 47-year-old woman presents seeking contraception. Her cycles were regular until 12 months ago and are now irregular with heavy bleeding and occasional hot flushes. She has 3 children by uncomplicated vaginal deliveries. Her BMI is 32 kg/m2, blood pressure is 148/92 on two readings, and she smokes 8 cigarettes a day. She has no personal history of VTE, breast cancer or migraine.

She does not wish to become pregnant, but she is bothered by menstrual heaviness (soaking a pad every 2 hours on the heaviest days) and mild vasomotor symptoms. She has not tried any hormonal method for 20 years. Her partner has had a vasectomy but they have separated and she has a new partner.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg (repeated), respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: BMI 32 kg/m2; abdomen soft with no mass; bimanual pelvic exam unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-160); ferritin 12 microgram/L (30-160); TSH within normal limits; urine bhCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line contraceptive option?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive containing ethinylestradiol 30 microgram and levonorgestrel
Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg intramuscular injection every 12 weeks
Levonorgestrel 52 mg intrauterine system for both contraception and heavy bleeding control
Vaginal ring containing ethinylestradiol and etonogestrel replaced every 21 days monthly
Copper intrauterine device inserted at the earliest opportunity in your consulting rooms

subtopic_detail: Suspected ovarian torsion imaging and management
stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 4 hours of sudden onset severe right lower quadrant pain associated with two episodes of vomiting. She reports intermittent similar but milder pain over the past 2 weeks that self-resolved within an hour. She is sexually active with a male partner using condoms; her last menstrual period was 10 days ago and was normal.

On examination she is uncomfortable and tender in the right adnexa without peritonism. A urinary bhCG is negative. Bedside ultrasound in ED shows an enlarged right ovary of 7.2 cm with peripherally displaced follicles and reduced arterial and venous Doppler flow compared with the left.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert; abdomen tender in right iliac fossa and right adnexa without peritonism or guarding; cervix closed on speculum; no purulent discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urinary bhCG negative; WCC 12.4 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 14 mg/L (<5); TVS: right ovary 7.2 cm with peripheral follicles and reduced Doppler flow

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for analgesia and observation with a repeat ultrasound in 12 hours to reassess
Intravenous ceftriaxone and doxycycline for empirical pelvic inflammatory disease cover
CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast to characterise the adnexal mass further
Urgent diagnostic laparoscopy and detorsion with ovarian preservation as the primary aim
Oophorectomy at open laparotomy without initial attempt at conservative detorsion

stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida is admitted to the day assessment unit at 9+2 weeks with a 3-week history of vomiting more than 8 times daily. She is unable to keep down oral fluids and has lost 4.5 kg from her booking weight of 62 kg (7 percent loss). Urine dipstick is positive for ketones 4+ and specific gravity is 1.030. Serum sodium is 137 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, urea 6.8 mmol/L.

She has already been prescribed pyridoxine 25 mg TDS and metoclopramide 10 mg TDS in the community for 5 days without benefit. She is not on any other medication. Thyroid function is within normal limits. Transvaginal ultrasound this morning shows a viable singleton with cardiac activity present.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick ketones 4+, specific gravity 1.030; sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 6.8 mmol/L (2.5-7.0); TSH within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Total parenteral nutrition via peripherally inserted central catheter for 2 weeks now
Increase metoclopramide to 20 mg oral four times daily and reassess in 48 hours at home
Commence oral prednisolone 40 mg daily as first-line escalation for symptom control
Consider medical termination of pregnancy at 9 weeks to end the underlying trigger
Admit for IV fluid resuscitation, ondansetron 4 mg IV 8 hourly and thiamine cover

stem:
A 30-year-old woman (G3P2) attends the antenatal clinic at 34 weeks to discuss her mode of delivery. Her first delivery was an emergency lower segment caesarean section for fetal distress at 8 cm dilatation at term. Her second delivery was an uncomplicated elective repeat lower segment caesarean at 39 weeks. She now wishes to attempt a vaginal birth after caesarean.

Her operative notes describe a low transverse uterine incision at both prior surgeries with no extension. She has a healthy singleton fetus in cephalic presentation, estimated fetal weight on the 55th centile, and adequate liquor. She has no other maternal medical problems. This antenatal clinic uses continuous intrapartum fetal monitoring and can offer immediate caesarean recovery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 138/min
data_table.Examination: Fundal height 34 cm; fetus cephalic; abdomen soft; scar Pfannenstiel well-healed
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound at 32 weeks: cephalic, EFW 55th centile, normal liquor; previous operative notes: two low transverse incisions without extension

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding mode of delivery?

options.text: Offer planned VBAC with continuous CTG monitoring in labour and one-to-one midwifery care
Two prior caesareans is an absolute contraindication and mandates elective caesarean now
Recommend induction of labour with prostaglandin E2 gel and titrated oxytocin infusion
Recommend home birth given her strong preference for a vaginal birth in this pregnancy
Arrange elective classical uterine incision caesarean at 37 weeks for safer scar assessment

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic plan when membranes rupture preterm in a known carrier
stem: A 27-year-old woman attends at 31 weeks after a gush of clear fluid two hours ago. She is not contracting and the first dose of betamethasone has been given.

data_table.Swab: Vagino-rectal swab at 30 weeks grew group B streptococcus
data_table.Findings: Pooled clear liquor, cervix closed, temperature 36.7 degC, normal cardiotocograph

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?

options.text: Oral erythromycin for ten days, with the penicillin held until labour
Intravenous benzylpenicillin four hourly from now until the baby is born
Oral erythromycin for ten days together with penicillin four hourly
Intravenous ampicillin and gentamicin, with birth expedited this evening
No antibiotic, with twice daily observations while awaiting spontaneous labour

stem:
A 32-year-old woman (G1P1) presents to the emergency department on day 4 postpartum after a spontaneous vaginal delivery complicated by a manual removal of retained placental tissue at the time of delivery. She reports 24 hours of fever, offensive-smelling vaginal discharge and lower abdominal pain. She is exclusively breastfeeding without any breast concerns.

On examination the fundus is 4 finger-breadths above the symphysis pubis and boggy, with cervical excitation and marked lower abdominal tenderness. She has no signs of skin infection at the perineum. She has no known drug allergies. She has not received antibiotics since delivery.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 39.0 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus tender, boggy, 4 fingerbreadths above symphysis; offensive lochia; cervical excitation; no perineal skin infection
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.1 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 168 mg/L (<5); lactate 3.2 mmol/L; blood cultures taken; endocervical swab sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic regimen?

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose alone until formal culture sensitivity is available
Oral amoxicillin/clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 days from ED discharge home
IV amoxicillin 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg plus gentamicin 5 mg/kg all 8-hourly
IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy as broad Gram negative and Gram positive cover
IV clindamycin 600 mg 8-hourly with intravenous fluids only as first-line therapy today

stem:
A 26-year-old primigravida with known type 1 von Willebrand disease is reviewed at 34 weeks in the combined obstetric-haematology clinic. Her sister has the same diagnosis. She has a history of heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche and prolonged bleeding after wisdom tooth extraction that responded to tranexamic acid and desmopressin.

Her third trimester coagulation screen today shows von Willebrand factor:antigen 92 IU/dL (50-150), von Willebrand factor:ristocetin cofactor activity 88 IU/dL (50-150), factor VIII activity 110 IU/dL (50-150). She has had an uncomplicated pregnancy so far. Baseline haemoglobin is 120 g/L and platelets are 240 x10^9/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, fundal height 34 cm, no bruising, no petechiae, no active bleeding
data_table.Investigations: VWF:Ag 92 IU/dL, VWF:RCo 88 IU/dL, FVIII 110 IU/dL; Hb 120 g/L; platelets 240 x10^9/L; fibrinogen 4.8 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate delivery plan?

options.text: Recommend termination of pregnancy given the significant peripartum bleeding risk exists
Elective caesarean section at 38 weeks under general anaesthesia to avoid regional block
Prophylactic von Willebrand factor concentrate infusion at onset of established labour
Plan vaginal delivery with active third stage and prophylactic tranexamic acid at delivery
Avoid all regional anaesthesia in labour due to unacceptable haematoma risk in this patient

stem:
A 27-year-old primigravida presents at 29+3 weeks with a sudden gush of clear fluid per vagina and a steady leak since. Sterile speculum examination confirms pooling of clear liquor in the posterior fornix. There are no contractions on the tocograph, the CTG is reactive and there is no vaginal bleeding or foul discharge.

She is afebrile and haemodynamically stable. Her white cell count is normal and CRP is unremarkable. A high vaginal swab is sent for microscopy and culture; group B streptococcus status is currently unknown. She has no known drug allergies. She has completed her first dose of betamethasone in ED.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Sterile speculum: pooling of clear liquor in the posterior fornix, cervix long and closed; no active bleeding; abdomen soft, non-tender
data_table.Investigations: WCC 9.4 x10^9/L (4-11); CRP 5 mg/L (<5); high vaginal swab sent; CTG reactive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate latency antibiotic regimen?

options.text: No antibiotics unless the patient develops fever or fetal tachycardia during the admission
Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 10 days from ED admission today
IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g every 4 hours until membrane rupture reaches 24 hours in duration
Oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days for anaerobic cover of the genital tract
Oral erythromycin 250 mg four times daily for 10 days or until delivery

stem:
A 29-year-old primigravida presents at 32+4 weeks with 6 hours of steady right upper quadrant pain, nausea and vomiting. Her booking blood pressure was 110/68 and today it is 138/86, then 132/82 on repeat 15 minutes later. She has no visual disturbance, headache or peripheral oedema. Urine dipstick shows trace protein and spot urine protein:creatinine ratio is 24 mg/mmol.

The obstetric registrar wondered aloud about biliary colic and requested an abdominal ultrasound which showed a normal gallbladder without stones and an unremarkable liver. Her platelet count 4 weeks ago was 245 x10^9/L. She has had no PV bleeding and the CTG is reactive. She feels fetal movements normally.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 132/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Examination: Alert, GCS 15, no papilloedema, no clonus, mild RUQ tenderness without guarding, no peripheral oedema; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-450); ALT 210 U/L (<40); AST 240 U/L (<40); LDH 620 U/L (<250); haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L; spot urine PCR 24 mg/mmol; blood film with schistocytes; INR within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis driving your management plan?

options.text: HELLP syndrome with delivery planned once corticosteroids are commenced and BP controlled
Acute fatty liver of pregnancy with plans for immediate broad hepatic support and delivery
Symptomatic gallstone pancreatitis given RUQ pain and elevated liver enzymes on presentation
Isolated pregnancy-related idiopathic thrombocytopenia (gestational) with likely spontaneous resolution
Viral hepatitis with expectant management and monitoring of fetal wellbeing over the next week

stem:
A 63-year-old woman presents to your general practice with 3 months of vague abdominal bloating and early satiety. She has no vaginal bleeding, no bowel disturbance and no urinary symptoms. Her last menstrual period was 12 years ago. Her mother had breast cancer at age 71 and her paternal aunt had ovarian cancer at age 58. She has no BRCA testing.

You arrange a pelvic ultrasound which shows a 6.2 cm left adnexal mass with 3 solid nodular papillary projections greater than 3 mm, thick internal septations and moderate colour flow. There is no free fluid and the right ovary is atrophic. Serum CA125 is 88 kU/L, serum HE4 elevated, and calculated risk of malignancy index (RMI) is 528.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74/min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild lower abdominal fullness, no ascites, no palpable mass; bimanual exam confirms left adnexal fullness
data_table.Investigations: TVS: 6.2 cm left adnexal mass with 3 papillary projections and thick septations; CA125 88 kU/L (<35); HE4 raised; RMI 528; family history as above

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat ultrasound in 3 months to observe any change in the mass or serum CA125 rise
Referral to a gynaecological oncology centre for surgical staging as the primary management
Referral to a general gynaecologist for laparoscopic ovarian cystectomy on the next list
Percutaneous ultrasound guided biopsy of the adnexal mass by an interventional radiologist
Empirical neoadjuvant carboplatin plus paclitaxel chemotherapy before any surgical intervention

stem:
A 31-year-old woman (G2P1) presents to your general practice at 25 weeks gestation for a routine antenatal review. She had a spontaneous conception, is on pregnancy multivitamins and iodine only, and has no diabetes symptoms. Her BMI at booking was 28 kg/m2. Her previous pregnancy was 3 years ago with an uneventful vaginal delivery at 39 weeks of a 3.4 kg baby and no documented GDM. She has no first-degree family history of diabetes.

A routine 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed today for universal screening returns fasting glucose 5.5 mmol/L, 1 hour glucose 9.8 mmol/L and 2 hour glucose 8.4 mmol/L. She has no symptoms of hyperglycaemia and her recent home blood pressures are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 25 cm; fetal heart rate 148/min; abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: 75 g OGTT fasting 5.5 mmol/L (ADIPS threshold 5.1); 1 hour 9.8 (10.0); 2 hour 8.4 (8.5); random urine dip negative for ketones

lead_in: How should you interpret and act on this OGTT?

options.text: Start metformin 500 mg twice daily today without any glucose monitoring or dietary intervention
Order an HbA1c today and only diagnose gestational diabetes if it is at or above 6.5 percent
Repeat the OGTT at 30 weeks because two values sit just below the ADIPS cut-offs on this test
Diagnose gestational diabetes now on the fasting glucose alone and start dietary and glucose monitoring pathway
Reassure that all values are below WHO diabetes cut-offs and no further action is needed today

stem:
A 30-year-old woman attends your general practice 4 weeks postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal birth of her first baby. She is exclusively breastfeeding on demand and has not resumed menstruation. Her blood pressure is normal, her BMI is 26 kg/m2, and she is a non-smoker. She has no personal or family history of VTE.

She wants long-acting contraception before returning to sexual activity, hoping to space her next pregnancy by at least 2 to 3 years. She is prepared to consider intrauterine or subdermal options and asks specifically about the effect of any hormonal method on her milk supply.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Well-healed second-degree perineal tear; uterus not palpable abdominally; lactating breasts with no mastitis
data_table.Investigations: Urine bhCG negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive plan today?

options.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate 150 mg IM given today with permanent bone density monitoring
Insert a copper IUD today and use condoms for the first 7 days as additional cover
Advise lactational amenorrhoea alone until the baby is 6 months old with no other method needed
Combined oral contraceptive pill starting today with 7 days condom use for cover
Etonogestrel subdermal implant inserted today with no need for additional contraceptive cover

stem:
A 33-year-old woman (G1P0) at 33+4 weeks presents to birth suite triage with a 3-day frontal headache and blurred vision this morning. She has attended all antenatal appointments and had normal BP throughout. Her booking BMI was 24 kg/m2. On arrival two seated BP readings are 168/112 and 166/108 five minutes apart. She is symptomatic and moderately distressed.

Urine dipstick is 3+ protein and a spot protein:creatinine ratio is 78 mg/mmol. Her platelets are 165 x10^9/L, ALT 34 U/L, creatinine 62 micromol/L. Fetal CTG shows a baseline of 145/min with normal variability and no decelerations, and the ultrasound is reassuring. She has taken no antihypertensives.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg then 166/108, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, fetal HR 145/min
data_table.Examination: Alert, orientated; brisk deep tendon reflexes; no clonus; mild bilateral leg oedema; abdomen soft with palpable fetal movements
data_table.Investigations: Urine dip 3+ protein; PCR 78 mg/mmol; platelets 165 x10^9/L; ALT 34 U/L; creatinine 62 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antihypertensive?

options.text: Oral labetalol 200 mg with a plan to repeat in 30 minutes if BP remains above 160/110
Oral atenolol 50 mg with plans for daily continuation until delivery
IV magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose before any antihypertensive is administered
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg for immediate rapid BP reduction and no monitoring escalation
Oral captopril 12.5 mg with the aim of BP reduction to 130/80 within 1 hour

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar called urgently to birth suite for a 34-year-old primigravid woman at 40+2 weeks in second stage. The head has just delivered but does not restitute and the shoulders have not descended after 45 seconds despite gentle downward traction. Her BMI is 33 kg/m2 and antenatal ultrasound estimated fetal weight 4.1 kg. The midwife has just called for help and switched on the emergency bell.

Maternal observations remain stable. The mother is in a semi-recumbent position with legs abducted. Fetal heart rate has been reassuring until now and is unavailable at this instant. You are the first doctor at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 96/min, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Fetal head delivered, no restitution, chin retracted against perineum (turtle sign); no visible cord
data_table.Investigations: Fetal heart rate not currently obtainable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first manoeuvre?

options.text: Direct routine episiotomy first regardless of soft tissue distensibility
McRoberts manoeuvre with hyperflexion of the hips and suprapubic pressure applied
Fundal pressure applied while continuing axial traction on the fetal head
Immediate Zavanelli manoeuvre to replace the head and proceed to caesarean section
Deliberate clavicular fracture of the anterior shoulder to reduce the bisacromial diameter

stem:
A 27-year-old woman (G1P0) presents to your regional maternity unit at 32+1 weeks with 3 hours of regular painful contractions every 4 to 5 minutes. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated to date. On speculum examination her cervix is 3 cm dilated and 80 percent effaced. Fetal fibronectin is not available in your unit. She has not received any antenatal corticosteroids in this pregnancy.

A fetal ultrasound performed on arrival shows a singleton cephalic presentation with an estimated fetal weight of 1.8 kg on the 45th centile. The CTG shows a baseline of 140/min with normal variability and no decelerations. Blood pressure is normal, urine is clean. There are no signs of chorioamnionitis and membranes are intact.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 88/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, 80 percent effaced; membranes intact; fetal head engaged
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 9 x10^9/L; CRP 4 mg/L; urinalysis clear; CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate tocolytic while corticosteroids and neuroprotection are given?

options.text: Oral indometacin 100 mg loading then 25 mg every 6 hours for a 48 hour course now
No tocolysis; proceed straight to delivery because dilation is beyond 3 cm
Oral nifedipine 20 mg loading then 20 mg every 30 minutes to a maximum of 40 mg in the first hour
IV salbutamol infusion at 5 microgram/min titrated to contractions and heart rate
IV atosiban 6.75 mg bolus then infusion for at least 24 hours as sole tocolytic

stem:
A 32-year-old woman (G2P1) attends your antenatal clinic at 36+2 weeks. Her first pregnancy was an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery. On palpation today the fetus feels breech and this is confirmed on point-of-care ultrasound: a frank breech, fetal back on the maternal left, adequate amniotic fluid volume and an anterior placenta clear of the lower segment. Estimated fetal weight is 2.9 kg on the 55th centile.

She has no scars on her uterus, no antepartum haemorrhage in this pregnancy, no known fetal abnormality and no evidence of ruptured membranes. Her booking BMI was 26 kg/m2 and her blood pressure has remained normal throughout. She wants to avoid caesarean if possible and asks about your recommendation for the next 2 weeks.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C, fetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Examination: Symphysio-fundal height 34 cm; frank breech confirmed on point-of-care ultrasound; adequate amniotic fluid; no palpable uterine tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: EFW 2.9 kg (55th centile); anterior placenta clear of lower segment; normal amniotic fluid index

lead_in: What is the most appropriate recommendation now?

options.text: Recommend vaginal breech delivery at 40 weeks without any attempt at ECV as the sole intervention
Advise moxibustion at the outer little toe alone as the primary intervention until 39 weeks
Perform ECV in the outpatient clinic today at 36+2 without tocolysis or CTG monitoring
Offer external cephalic version at 37 weeks with tocolysis and continuous fetal monitoring in the birth suite
Book elective caesarean section for 39 weeks without discussing external cephalic version

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar on-call and are called urgently at 03:15 to a 28-year-old multipara at 39+5 weeks in the birth suite. She has just had spontaneous rupture of membranes with a moderate gush of clear liquor. The midwife immediately palpates a soft pulsatile cord in the vagina at the introitus. The CTG shows a prolonged fetal deceleration to 80/min for the last 3 minutes with poor variability, having previously been reactive.

The patient is a spontaneous labourer with cervix now 6 cm dilated, fetal head at the pelvic inlet, station -2. Full theatre team is stood by and anaesthetist is 8 minutes away by phone. She has been prepared for anaesthesia (fasting 6 hours). She has no significant medical history and no cardiovascular contraindications.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 100/min, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, fetal heart rate 80/min for 3 minutes
data_table.Examination: Cord palpable and pulsating at introitus; cervix 6 cm dilated; head at -2 station; membranes ruptured
data_table.Investigations: Group and save on file; last Hb 128 g/L (115-160); no pre-existing coagulopathy

lead_in: Which single set of pre-transfer measures should you undertake now to maximise fetal survival before theatre?

options.text: Reduce the cord back through the cervix with a warm saline soaked pack and continue augmentation of labour with routine outpatient follow-up
Continue oxytocin augmentation to achieve rapid vaginal delivery of the head while she is still 6 cm with routine outpatient follow-up
Apply Kielland forceps to expedite vaginal delivery from -2 station with pudendal block only with standard supportive measures alongside
Perform emergency symphysiotomy in the birth suite while awaiting the anaesthetist to arrive with standard supportive measures alongside
Elevate the presenting part manually and place her in knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position with a filled 500 mL bladder catheter and IV tocolysis if delivery is likely delayed

stem:
You are the O and G registrar in a metropolitan tertiary hospital. A 34-year-old woman (G4P3) delivered a 4.3 kg baby 45 minutes ago after a spontaneous labour induced for postdates. She had a manually removed placenta for retained placenta. Her booking bloods showed normal Hb and platelets. She has ongoing haemorrhage now totalling 2500 mL despite: Syntocinon 10 unit IM at delivery, Syntocinon 40 unit infusion running, ergometrine 250 microgram IM after 15 minutes, carboprost 250 microgram IM after 25 minutes, misoprostol 800 microgram PR, tranexamic acid 1 g IV, bimanual compression, empty bladder, and 2 units of packed cells running.

Her uterus remains soft and above the umbilicus. Speculum inspection is negative for genital tract trauma. Coagulation testing 10 minutes ago showed fibrinogen 1.9 g/L (2.0-4.5), platelets 78 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, temperature 35.4 degrees C. Consultant is 15 minutes away. Theatre is available now.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, blood pressure 84/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 97 percent on 6 L oxygen, temperature 35.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft, 2 cm above umbilicus; no visible genital tract trauma on speculum; bladder empty via IDC
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 1.9 g/L (2.0-4.5); platelets 78 x10^9/L; INR 1.4; venous lactate 4.6 mmol/L; running 2 units PRBC

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step now?

options.text: Transfer to theatre for intrauterine balloon tamponade with continued transfusion and activation of massive transfusion protocol
Repeat carboprost 250 microgram IM every 15 minutes until 8 doses are given regardless of hypertension
Repeat tranexamic acid 1 g IV every 30 minutes without other escalation until bleeding stops as the sole intervention
Immediate hysterectomy in the birth suite without prior balloon tamponade or interventional radiology
Continue current transfusion at the current rate and observe for another 30 minutes before further action

stem:
You are the GP shared-care doctor reviewing a 34-year-old woman at 27 weeks gestation with her first pregnancy. She has no personal history of diabetes but her mother has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin. Her booking BMI was 29 kg/m2. She has had no antenatal complications so far and fetal movements are normal.

Her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 26 weeks reports fasting plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L, 1 hour plasma glucose 9.6 mmol/L and 2 hour plasma glucose 8.3 mmol/L. She is asymptomatic. Fetal biometry today shows growth appropriate for gestation with an abdominal circumference on the 60th centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Symphyseal-fundal height 27 cm, fetal heart rate 148/min
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 5.4 mmol/L (<5.1); 1 hour 9.6 mmol/L (<10.0); 2 hour 8.3 mmol/L (<8.5); HbA1c 5.6 percent

lead_in: Which of the following best describes the interpretation and next management step?

options.text: Normal OGTT; continue routine antenatal care and repeat OGTT only if polyhydramnios or macrosomia develops later
Impaired glucose tolerance; repeat OGTT at 32 weeks and defer any dietary intervention until that repeat test
Overt diabetes in pregnancy; start immediate insulin therapy without a trial of lifestyle and dietary modification
GDM; refer to a diabetes-in-pregnancy service, start diet and lifestyle change and begin glucose self-monitoring
GDM; commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately as first-line without an initial dietary trial period

subtopic_detail: Advice for future pregnancies after a baby with early onset sepsis
stem: A 32-year-old woman attends for a debrief six weeks after her first baby was treated in the neonatal unit. She asks what would be different in a future pregnancy.

data_table.Index birth: Term vaginal birth, blood culture on day one grew group B streptococcus
data_table.Today: Mother and baby both well, no allergies, no other complications

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: She will be offered antibiotics in every future labour whatever a swab shows
She will be swabbed at 36 weeks and treated only if that swab is positive
She will be offered a planned caesarean section to avoid the birth canal
She will need an oral antibiotic through the whole third trimester next time
Nothing changes, because this was a single event unlikely to happen again

stem:
You are the on-call registrar. A 31-year-old woman with severe pre-eclampsia has just had a spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks. She had labetalol running throughout and her most recent blood pressure was 158/102 mmHg. Placenta was delivered spontaneously and appears complete on inspection. Estimated blood loss so far is 1200 mL and continues to flow briskly.

On examination the fundus is boggy but there is no obvious trauma. Bimanual compression is initiated by your midwifery colleague and intravenous access is confirmed patent. Uterine massage produces a small transient contraction. Bloods are being sent. The patient is alert and speaking but pale. IV oxytocin 10 units has been given as part of active management and a further 40 units infusion in 1 litre normal saline is running.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 158/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus, no visible tear on speculum, moderate ongoing dark blood loss, bimanual compression in progress
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1200 mL and continuing; Hb pending; group and hold sent; coagulation panel pending

lead_in: Which uterotonic is the most appropriate next agent given her clinical picture?

options.text: Carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses
Ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular repeat once as second-line agent after ongoing oxytocin infusion
Syntometrine 1 mL intramuscular containing 5 units oxytocin and 500 microgram ergometrine combined
Misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual and re-dose at 60 minutes if bleeding persists
Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous as monotherapy in place of additional uterotonic agents

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar receiving a 28-year-old G1P0 woman at 30+2 weeks gestation from a rural transfer with regular painful contractions for 4 hours. Speculum shows cervix 3 cm dilated with intact membranes. Fetal fibronectin was positive on the referring hospital assessment. She has no vaginal bleeding, no fever and no history of asthma. Booking blood pressure was 108/68 mmHg and today's is 118/72 mmHg. Fetal heart rate on continuous cardiotocography is reassuring with baseline 145/min and normal variability.

She has already received the first dose of intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg. Neonatal intensive care is available on site. Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection is being prepared. She has no drug allergies and no significant past medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Regular contractions every 3 minutes; cervix 3 cm dilated 60 percent effaced; membranes intact; cephalic presentation
data_table.Investigations: Fetal fibronectin positive; fetal cardiotocography baseline 145/min normal variability; full blood count within normal limits; urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: Which tocolytic is the most appropriate first-line choice to buy time for corticosteroid completion and transfer?

options.text: Salbutamol 100 microgram intravenous infusion titrated to slow contractions over the next 12 hours
Nifedipine 20 mg oral immediate release stat, then 20 mg every 30 minutes for two further doses if contractions persist
Atosiban 6.75 mg intravenous bolus then 300 microgram per minute infusion for 3 hours as first-line agent
Indometacin 100 mg per rectum then 25 mg every 6 hours for 48 hours as tocolysis regardless of the gestation involved
Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous loading dose then 1 g per hour as combined tocolysis and neuroprotection

subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy with prior contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
A 33-year-old woman with a G3P1 obstetric history presents to your gynaecology emergency clinic with right-sided pelvic pain and light PV spotting for 24 hours. Her last menstrual period was 6+3 weeks ago. Two years ago she had a laparoscopic left salpingectomy for a ruptured left tubal ectopic. She and her partner have been actively trying to conceive for the past 8 months. She is haemodynamically stable and has no shoulder tip pain.

On examination she has right adnexal tenderness without peritonism. Her serum beta hCG is 3200 IU/L today, and a repeat 48 hours ago was 1900 IU/L. Transvaginal ultrasound today shows an empty uterus with an endometrium of 12 mm, a 2.4 cm right tubal mass without fetal cardiac activity and a small amount of free pelvic fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Full blood count and coagulation are within normal limits. She has no significant medical history and no allergies. Her body surface area is calculated at 1.75 m2.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right adnexal tenderness without peritonism; cervix closed on speculum; scant blood in vagina; no shoulder tip pain
data_table.Investigations: beta hCG 3200 IU/L (today) rising from 1900 IU/L (48 hours ago); TVUS empty uterus, right tubal 2.4 cm mass no cardiac activity, small pouch of Douglas free fluid; Hb 128 g/L (115-165); coagulation within normal limits; body surface area 1.75 m2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Expectant management with beta hCG surveillance twice weekly aiming for spontaneous resolution over 2-4 weeks
Single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre body surface area with day 4 and 7 beta hCG
Laparoscopic right salpingostomy with careful haemostasis and post-operative beta hCG surveillance
Laparoscopic right salpingectomy as definitive treatment given the ectopic in the sole remaining tube
Ultrasound-guided intra-sac methotrexate injection under transvaginal guidance today

stem:
You are the obstetric registrar reviewing a 26-year-old G1P0 at 33+4 weeks gestation admitted overnight with hypertension. Her booking blood pressure was 108/68 mmHg. Overnight she has developed severe headache resistant to paracetamol, epigastric pain and reduced urine output. She has had no seizures. Fetal movements are reduced. Cardiotocography shows a baseline of 155/min with reduced variability but no decelerations.

Investigations show blood pressure 168/112 mmHg after two doses of intravenous labetalol 20 mg. Platelets are 82 x10^9/L (150-450), creatinine has risen from 62 micromol/L at booking to 118 micromol/L (45-90), ALT 148 U/L (<45), urinary protein-creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol (<30). Urine output has been 25 mL/hour for the last 4 hours. She has had 1 g magnesium sulfate loading given 30 minutes ago. Her partner is at the bedside. Fetal biometry today shows growth on the 15th centile with normal umbilical artery Doppler.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 168/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, fetal HR 155/min
data_table.Examination: Alert but distressed, brisk deep tendon reflexes without clonus, right upper quadrant tenderness, no papilloedema on fundoscopy, symphysio-fundal height 30 cm
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-450); creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90) rising from 62; ALT 148 U/L (<45); urinary protein-creatinine ratio 380 mg/mmol (<30); urine output 25 mL/h for 4 hours; CTG baseline 155/min reduced variability

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Continue intravenous labetalol and reassess blood pressure and urine output in another 2 hours before deciding on delivery
Give a further intravenous fluid bolus of 500 mL normal saline for oliguria and titrate the antihypertensive to target
Cease magnesium sulfate loading dose because platelets under 100 x10^9/L are a contraindication to magnesium
Give first dose of antenatal corticosteroid and plan delivery within 24-48 hours after stabilising blood pressure
Perform emergency caesarean section under general anaesthesia without waiting for corticosteroid effect

stem:
A 28-year-old woman attends your general practice for a routine cervical screening test. She has had one previous negative test at age 25. She has no post-coital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding or vaginal discharge. She is up to date with HPV vaccination from a school program. She has a new male partner and uses combined oral contraception. Her last menstrual period was 12 days ago.

The cervical screening test (CST) reports oncogenic HPV positive (non-16/18 types) with reflex liquid-based cytology showing possible low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (pLSIL). Speculum examination at the time of collection showed a clinically normal cervix with no contact bleeding or visible lesion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Speculum: clinically normal cervix, no contact bleeding, no visible lesion
data_table.Investigations: CST oncogenic HPV positive (non-16/18); reflex LBC possible low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management according to the National Cervical Screening Program?

options.text: Repeat cervical screening test in 6 months and refer to colposcopy only if oncogenic HPV persists at that visit
Refer to colposcopy within 8 weeks because the reflex cytology reports low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion
Refer to gynaecology for LLETZ excision because possible LSIL requires immediate treatment to prevent progression
Return to routine 5-yearly screening because HPV vaccination status makes progression to invasive cancer negligible
Repeat oncogenic HPV test in 12 months and refer to colposcopy if oncogenic HPV persists at that repeat

subtopic_detail: Uterine rupture recognition in VBAC labour
stem:
You are called to the birth suite for a 34-year-old G3P2 woman at 39+5 weeks gestation undergoing a planned vaginal birth after caesarean. Her previous caesarean two years ago was for breech at term with a low transverse incision and uncomplicated recovery. Her first birth was a normal vaginal delivery. Labour has been augmented with a low-dose oxytocin infusion for slow progress from 6 cm dilatation, and she has an epidural in situ. She is currently 8 cm dilated.

Continuous cardiotocography over the last 20 minutes shows late decelerations to 90/min with slow recovery. She reports a new severe suprapubic tearing pain between contractions that broke through her epidural, and there is a small amount of fresh vaginal bleeding. The presenting part is felt at station -1 on vaginal examination now, whereas 20 minutes ago it was at station 0. Her blood pressure has dropped from 118/72 to 92/58 mmHg over the last 10 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: New suprapubic tearing pain breaking through epidural; fresh PV bleeding; presenting part regressed from 0 to -1 station
data_table.Investigations: CTG late decelerations to 90/min with slow recovery; fetal baseline 165/min; oxytocin infusion running

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Cease oxytocin infusion and prepare for immediate category 1 caesarean section
Increase oxytocin infusion to strengthen contractions and re-examine in 30 minutes
Give a further epidural bolus for pain and continue expectant management to full dilatation
Apply a fetal scalp electrode and take a fetal blood sample to confirm distress before decision
Attempt an assisted vaginal delivery with ventouse to expedite birth given cervical dilation of 8 cm

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 at 39+2 weeks is admitted to your regional birth suite for artificial rupture of membranes to augment prolonged latent labour. Immediately after rupture, a loop of pulsating cord is felt below the presenting part at the introitus. Her previous births were normal vaginal deliveries at term. The fetus is estimated at 3.4 kg on scan last week.

On examination the vertex is at station -2 and the cervix is 5 cm dilated with a soft tucked-in loop of cord clearly palpable in front of the head. The mother is anxious but comfortable. Continuous cardiotocography shows a fetal heart rate baseline of 90/min with deep prolonged decelerations. The on-call obstetric registrar is 4 minutes away and the anaesthetist is at the head of the bed. The theatre team is being activated with a Category 1 caesarean call.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 108/min, blood pressure 128/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C; fetal heart rate 90/min with prolonged decelerations
