data_table.Examination: Cord palpable below the presenting part at the introitus, cervix 5 cm dilated, vertex station -2
data_table.Investigations: Cardiotocography as above; pre-existing group and hold in place

lead_in: While waiting for theatre, what is the single most appropriate immediate manoeuvre?

options.text: Ask the mother to bear down with the next contraction to complete a rapid spontaneous vaginal birth in the birth room without transfer to theatre
Give a single intravenous dose of ergometrine 250 micrograms to expel the fetus rapidly through the cervix as a temporising measure
Cut and clamp the prolapsed cord at the introitus to prevent further cord exposure and vasospasm during the transfer to theatre
Elevate the presenting part with the examining hand, place the mother in knee-chest position and fill the bladder with 500 mL warm saline via catheter
Start intravenous oxytocin infusion at 12 milliunits per minute to accelerate labour and shorten time to delivery

subtopic_detail: GBS intrapartum prophylaxis with penicillin allergy
stem:
A 29-year-old G2P1 at 39+0 weeks is admitted to your metropolitan birth suite in early spontaneous labour. Her routine antenatal vagino-rectal swab at 36 weeks was positive for group B streptococcus. She has a documented history of anaphylaxis to penicillin at age 12, treated with intramuscular adrenaline, and has never been formally allergy tested since. She has no known allergy to clindamycin or vancomycin. Her previous birth in New Zealand was uncomplicated with intrapartum benzylpenicillin, which she cannot recall clearly.

On examination she is comfortable, cervix is 4 cm dilated and effaced, membranes intact, vertex presentation at station 0. Contractions are every 4 minutes lasting 40 seconds. Cardiotocography is reassuring. Her medical notes flag the anaphylaxis with a red bracelet. Local antimicrobial stewardship policy requires you to give intrapartum prophylaxis to this patient.

data_table.Vital signs: Maternal pulse 92/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C; fetal heart rate 138/min baseline, reassuring
data_table.Examination: Cervix 4 cm dilated, effaced, membranes intact, vertex at station 0
data_table.Investigations: 36-week vagino-rectal swab positive for group B streptococcus; sensitivity report not available

lead_in: What is the most appropriate intrapartum antibiotic choice?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery with adrenaline available at the bedside
Intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every 8 hours until delivery because cephalosporin cross-reactivity is under 2 percent
Oral azithromycin 500 mg once at admission as an equivalent alternative to intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis
No antibiotic prophylaxis, and observe the neonate for 48 hours with early paediatric review given the maternal allergy history
Intravenous vancomycin 20 mg per kilogram (maximum 2 g) infused over 2 hours, repeated every 8 hours until delivery

stem:
A 34-year-old G2P1 has just delivered a live female infant of 3.6 kg at 40+3 weeks by unassisted vaginal birth in your regional birth suite. Her pregnancy was uncomplicated except for gestational hypertension controlled on labetalol 200 mg twice daily, with blood pressures around 130/85 mmHg over the last month. Her first delivery 3 years ago was complicated by a primary postpartum haemorrhage of 1.5 litres treated with a bimanual uterine compression and further uterotonics.

Cord clamping was delayed by 90 seconds and the baby is doing skin-to-skin on her chest. The placenta has not yet delivered. She has an intravenous cannula in place and observations are stable. She has no known drug allergy and is not asthmatic. The midwife is preparing to administer the routine third-stage uterotonic and asks you which agent to draw up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 132/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus at umbilicus, small trickle of blood at the introitus, no active haemorrhage
data_table.Investigations: Not required before uterotonic administration

lead_in: What is the most appropriate uterotonic to administer now?

options.text: Intramuscular oxytocin 10 units into the anterolateral thigh as prophylactic active management of the third stage
Intramuscular Syntometrine (ergometrine 500 micrograms plus oxytocin 5 units) as combined prophylactic active management
Rectal misoprostol 800 micrograms as an equivalent to intramuscular oxytocin for prophylactic third-stage management
Intravenous carboprost 250 micrograms slow push as prophylactic uterotonic in women at risk of postpartum haemorrhage
Withhold routine uterotonic and use physiological management given the delayed cord clamping already performed

subtopic_detail: Tubal ectopic surgical choice after contralateral salpingectomy
stem:
A 33-year-old G3P1 is admitted to your metropolitan gynaecology unit at 7+2 weeks by dates with lower abdominal pain and light vaginal spotting for 12 hours. She had a right salpingectomy 4 years ago for a ruptured tubal ectopic that presented with haemorrhagic shock. She conceived spontaneously this cycle and is desperate to preserve future fertility. She has no history of pelvic inflammatory disease and no ongoing medications.

On examination she is haemodynamically stable but pale, with left iliac fossa tenderness and cervical excitation. Serum beta-hCG is 6800 IU/L and rising 60 percent from a level 48 hours ago. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a 3.0 cm adnexal mass adjacent to the ipsilateral (left) ovary with fetal cardiac activity and a small volume of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Her partner is present and understands the situation. She has requested surgical management as she cannot commit to weekly follow-up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale, left iliac fossa tenderness, cervical excitation, no rebound
data_table.Investigations: Serum beta-hCG 6800 IU/L; TVUSS: empty uterus, 3.0 cm left adnexal mass with fetal cardiac activity, small pouch of Douglas fluid; blood group A positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate surgical management?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy on the left tube to preserve tubal function and future spontaneous fertility with weekly beta-hCG follow-up
Laparoscopic salpingectomy on the left tube with counselling about need for in vitro fertilisation for future conception
Single-dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre with weekly beta-hCG follow-up until non-pregnant range
Expectant management with 48-hourly beta-hCG monitoring while she considers her options over the coming week
Laparotomy with total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for definitive management

stem:
A 36-year-old G2P2 is reviewed on the postnatal ward day 3 after an uncomplicated spontaneous vaginal delivery at 39+5 weeks. Her antenatal course was unremarkable, blood pressures always below 130/80 mmHg and no proteinuria. Today she reports right upper quadrant pain, nausea and one episode of vomiting for the last 12 hours. She has been well hydrated and has been mobilising.

On examination she is diaphoretic. Right upper quadrant is tender without peritonism, uterus is well contracted and lochia is normal. Reflexes are 3+ with two beats of clonus at the right ankle. There is no rash. Her recent bloods show haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-160), platelets 62 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 480 U/L (5-30), AST 520 U/L (10-40), LDH 780 U/L (110-250), creatinine 118 micromol/L (45-90), fibrinogen 3.4 g/L (1.5-4.0), INR 1.1 (0.9-1.2) and urine dipstick 3+ protein. A blood film shows fragmented red cells.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 178/112 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, right upper quadrant tender without peritonism, hyperreflexia with clonus, uterus contracted, normal lochia
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L (115-160); platelets 62 x10^9/L (150-400); ALT 480 U/L (5-30); AST 520 U/L (10-40); LDH 780 U/L (110-250); creatinine 118 mcmol/L (45-90); fibrinogen 3.4 g/L (1.5-4.0); urine 3+ protein; blood film fragments

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg empirically for suspected postnatal endometritis and cholangitis
Intramuscular ergometrine 250 micrograms and firm uterine fundal massage for suspected occult postpartum haemorrhage
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g load then 1 g per hour infusion plus intravenous labetalol 20 mg for blood pressure control
Urgent abdominal ultrasound looking for gallstones and biliary dilatation before starting any specific therapy for her presentation
Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days to accelerate platelet recovery in postpartum HELLP

stem:
A 30-year-old G3P2 at 32+4 weeks presents to your regional birth suite with sudden severe constant lower abdominal pain and 400 mL of dark vaginal bleeding for 30 minutes. She smokes 15 cigarettes daily. Her antenatal ultrasound at 20 weeks reported a fundal placenta. She has hypertension in this pregnancy managed on labetalol 200 mg twice daily.

On examination she is pale and clammy, uterus is woody hard and tender between contractions, with tender points more marked over the left uterine wall. Fetal parts are difficult to palpate. Cardiotocography shows late decelerations with reduced variability and a fetal heart rate baseline of 110/min. Speculum reveals dark blood at the introitus, cervix appears closed. Point-of-care coagulation shows fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.0-4.5), platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400) and INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2). A pre-existing group and hold is on file. Two large-bore intravenous lines have been sited.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97 percent on 6 L/min via face mask, temperature 36.7 degrees C; fetal heart rate 110/min with late decelerations
data_table.Examination: Pale and clammy, woody hard tender uterus, fetal parts difficult to palpate, closed cervix on speculum, dark vaginal blood
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L (115-160); fibrinogen 1.4 g/L (2.0-4.5); platelets 92 x10^9/L (150-400); INR 1.4 (0.9-1.2); group A positive; crossmatch requested

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Transabdominal ultrasound in the birth suite to confirm placental location before any further intervention today
Nifedipine 20 mg orally to tocolyse for 48 hours plus intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg for fetal lung maturation
Await further fetal cardiotocography over the next hour to confirm sustained pathological trace before mobilising theatre
Activate the massive transfusion protocol, correct coagulopathy with fibrinogen concentrate, and proceed to Category 1 caesarean delivery
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes as neuroprotection while awaiting further imaging results

subtopic_detail: Amniotic fluid embolism vs pulmonary embolism
stem:
A 34-year-old G3P2 at 39+6 weeks is in the second stage of labour after augmentation with intravenous oxytocin. As the head crowns she suddenly complains of feeling short of breath, becomes profoundly cyanotic and loses consciousness within 60 seconds. She had no known respiratory or cardiac history, no prior thromboembolism and no obesity. Prophylactic enoxaparin was ceased in early labour per protocol.

CPR is commenced immediately and a Code Blue is called. Bag-mask ventilation is difficult due to central cyanosis and pink frothy secretions from the mouth. Rhythm strip shows pulseless electrical activity. There is heavy vaginal blood loss estimated at 1200 mL in the last few minutes with no obvious source on inspection. Point-of-care coagulation shows fibrinogen 1.0 g/L (2.0-4.5), INR 2.4 (0.9-1.2) and platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400). Bedside transthoracic echocardiography by the anaesthetic registrar shows a dilated dyskinetic right ventricle with septal bowing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulseless electrical activity, no measurable blood pressure, SpO2 unrecordable on 15 L/min via bag-mask, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Cyanotic, unresponsive, pink frothy oral secretions, heavy vaginal blood loss, dilated tender uterus
data_table.Investigations: Fibrinogen 1.0 g/L (2.0-4.5); INR 2.4 (0.9-1.2); platelets 68 x10^9/L (150-400); TTE dilated dyskinetic right ventricle with septal bowing

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step alongside ongoing advanced life support?

options.text: Systemic thrombolysis with intravenous alteplase 100 mg infused over 90 minutes for suspected massive pulmonary embolism as the primary cause
Intravenous adrenaline 5 mg bolus every 3 to 5 minutes to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure during the ongoing cardiac arrest
Insert a right internal jugular central venous oximetry catheter before any operative decision so that resuscitation therapy can be titrated
Continue closed-chest CPR alone and defer perimortem caesarean until return of spontaneous maternal circulation is confirmed on the rhythm strip
Perimortem caesarean at 4 minutes, activate massive transfusion with fibrinogen concentrate, and give inhaled pulmonary vasodilator for right ventricular support
